message.content:
**Freezing point of pure water at 10 kPa**

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Pressure** | \(10\;\text{kPa}\) (about one‑tenth of atmospheric pressure) |
| **Calculated freezing point** | \(\approx 0.00^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) |

---

### Why the change is negligible

At standard atmospheric pressure (\(p_{\!atm}=101.3\,\text{kPa}\)) the melting/freeze point of pure water is exactly \(0^\circ\text{C}\).

For temperatures near this point the ice–liquid equilibrium follows the Clausius–Clapeyron relation:

\[
\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}
   = \frac{\Delta H_\text{fus}}{T\,\Delta V},
\qquad
\Rightarrow 
\quad
\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}
   = \frac{T\,\Delta V}{\Delta H_\text{fus}}
\]

Using:
* \(T\simeq 273\,\text{K}\)
* Enthalpy of fusion \(\Delta H_\text{fus}\simeq 3.34\times10^{5}\,\text{J·kg}^{-1}\)
* Density difference \(\rho_{liq}-\rho_{solid}\simeq 83\,\text{kg·m}^{-3}\)

gives  

\[
\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\approx 7\times10^{-5}\;
      ^\circ\!\text{C}/\text{kPa}.
\]

A pressure decrease from 101 kPa to 10 kPa corresponds to a reduction of  
\(91\,\text{kPa}\times 7\times10^{-5}\,^∘\text{C/kPa}\approx 0.006^\circ\text{C}\).

So even under a tenfold pressure drop the freezing point shifts by only a few thousandths of a degree—well beyond ordinary measurement precision.

---

#### Bottom line

Under normal laboratory conditions you may safely treat the freezing point of water at 10 kPa as **exactly 0 °C**, acknowledging an uncertainty far smaller than \(±0.01^\circ\text{C}\).
